tldr: Mid-October arXiv papers began framing long-horizon agent work around research-state tracking and continual-learning benchmarks. Late October added search evaluation with failure localization, critic-based credit assignment, and memory governance.
whats_new: JHiMA-WebRL applies joint hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning to long-horizon web tasks, following a paper questioning whether long-horizon terminal benchmarks are actually deep.
why_it_matters: Long-horizon failures (lost state, stale memory, weak credit assignment) are what break production agents; this cluster shows research moving from raw task length toward diagnosing where trajectories fail.

beats.headline: Research state and continual learning define the problem
beats.summary: ClueFlow models search as attributed state transitions; Continual Learning Exam benchmarks experiential learning.

beats.headline: Failure localization, critics and memory governance
beats.summary: Papers target where long trajectories break: search failure nodes, sparse-reward credit, and outdated memories.

beats.headline: Multi-agent collaboration and a benchmark-depth critique
beats.summary: Goal-aware collaboration arrives alongside a challenge to how benchmark length is measured.

beats.headline: Hierarchical multi-agent RL for web tasks

open_questions: Do any of these methods report results on a deployed agent rather than a research benchmark?
Does the benchmark-depth critique change how later long-horizon papers measure task length?
Do JHiMA-WebRL or CALM release code or cost and latency measurements?
take_for_builders: If you evaluate long-running agents, track failure nodes and memory staleness rather than turn counts alone; these are unreplicated preprints, so rerun on your own tasks before adopting any method.
